title: CLO 2025 Course: Unlock New Styles in Denim, CLO Technical Experts Teach You How to Master Washed Denim!
description:
Master Denim Washing Design!  
Using CLO 2025.1 Denim Washing Process Presets, CLO technical experts will guide you step-by-step on how to master the new features. Instantly transform basic styles into designer pieces, achieving denim wash effects from classic to avant-garde, completing the entire look.  
Reply "Free Materials" in the "CLO3D" WeChat official account inbox to receive this issue's learning materials.
transcript:
Today, I'm going to show you how to make a denim water-wash costume.  
In this process, I will demonstrate how to transform a simple basic shirt into a jacket as shown in the picture.  
First, open the CLO app.  
If you have downloaded the materials, you can upload them into the project.  
I will upload them here since I have already downloaded them in advance.  
You can reply with "denim water wash" to the public account to download the materials.  

After opening our materials, import a basic style shirt file first.  
Let's start modifying it.  
The style to be changed includes:  
- A single panel at the bottom  
- A relatively wider placket (door)  
- The upper and front body are divided vertically  
- Two vertical cuts on the lower half  
- Designs of the pocket and belt cover  

Next, let's adjust the style.  
Open the 3D window to observe.  
The length is generally suitable, but if you want to add a new panel at the bottom, you can make the shirt shorter.  
I'm using the Edit Pattern tool.  
Select the bottom edges of the front and back panels, then move them up or down.  
When moving, right-click to enter a specific distance. Here, I enter 55.  
You can adjust the length as needed.  

After the change, measure the total length of the bottom edge.  
Using the Edit Pattern tool (shortcut key Z), I select all bottom edges at once.  
The total length is 638.2.  
Now, redraw the bottom panel using the Shape tool (shortcut key S).  
In the 2D window’s blank area, input 638.2.  
If your length differs, measure accordingly.  
Align this panel using the Edit Pattern tool.  
This completes the bottom panel.  

Now, sew the panels together.  
You can use free sewing or segment sewing.  
Sew the bottom to the front and back panels, including the placket area.  
I sewed half, then symmetrically duplicated the other half.  

Go back to the 3D window.  
Use the Adjustment Pattern tool to move the panel if necessary.  
Right-click on this panel and add it to the side to position it close to the sewn panel.  
Then simulate the garment.  

Next, add buttons and buttonholes on the bottom panel near the placket.  
Refer to the position of the placket above.  
Select the middle line of the placket with the Edit Pattern tool; the center should be the midpoint.  
The left side is half, 20 mm.  
Buttons should be placed 20 mm from the edge.  

Find the Button tool in the 3D toolbar on the left.  
Right-click on the panel to add a left button.  
A movable window appears where you can set the button’s distance from the top and bottom edges.  
Set the left distance to 20 mm, and the top to half the panel height (27.5 mm).  

Switch to the Select Movable Button tool.  
You can see the button as an eye on the surface in the 3D window.  
Right-click the button to convert it into an eye.  
Then right-click again to copy the button to the symmetrical panel.  
Copy it over.  

Use the Button tool below to combine them by clicking the button and then the eye.  
This creates a small lock in 3D, representing the button-eye connection.  

Next, modify the placket.  
If the placket is narrow and you want it wider, merge the existing placket division lines, then redraw a wider division line.  
Use the Edit Pattern tool (Z) to select the division lines and merge them.  
Now the placket width is 40 mm (20 + 20).  
You can add 20 mm wider on the right side.  

Right-click the division line and set the distance from the left edge to 20 mm, matching the bottom panel’s placket width.  
Draw a vertical line on the right using the Internal Multi-Line tool (shortcut G), holding Shift to ensure verticality.  
Double-click at the top to finish.  

Use the Edit Pattern tool, right-click, and select Cut and Sew to finalize the placket division.  

Now the width of the placket has been changed.  
Next, we will adjust the upper and lower segments of the front panel.  
The front panel has a hollow line in the middle, visible in the design.  
Use the Hook and Loop tool to cut and sew this line with the base line.  

For the placket, manually draw a horizontal inner line using the Internal Multi-Line tool, starting and ending with the left mouse button where there is a small hollow line.  
Select both lines with the Hook and Loop tool and right-click to Cut and Sew.  

After division, move the front panel to the right side of the screen.  
The division line may look jagged now.  
Use the Curve Edit tool to smooth it by converting corner points to curve points or deleting excess curve points.  
Adjust the curve points as needed for a smooth shape.  

Next, divide the large panel below the front panel.  
It has two vertical dividing lines and includes a pocket and belt cover.  
Use the Plus Point Division tool (shortcut X).  
Right-click the lower line and input 65 mm on the left and 25 mm on the right.  
Right-click the upper line and input 30 mm and 90 mm for the first and second segments.  

Based on these divisions, draw two vertical lines with the Internal Multi-Line tool.  
After drawing, draw the pocket pattern slightly wider than the vertical lines.  
Use the Plus Point Division tool and input 125 mm for the pocket’s height or side length.  

Use the Edit Pattern tool to select the narrow lines of the divisions.  
Right-click the internal line diameter and set it to 10 mm without extension.  
Check if the ends of the two lines connect with the outer edge of the panel to ensure a closed shape.  
Select both ends with Shift, right-click, and add points to the outer edge.  
Complete the pocket shape by creating a middle line between the two vertical lines.  
Right-click between the lines to create an inner line and align it with the outer edge.  

To adjust the pocket’s position, use the Edit Pattern tool.  
In 3D, enable the inner line display to see the pocket’s shape and position.  
Pull the pocket slightly wider at the bottom by dragging along the line while pressing the Control key to create a smooth elliptical curve.  
Extend it 10 mm outward on both sides.  

Next, create the belt cover similarly.  
Use the Plus Point Division tool to set diameters of 30 mm and 20 mm on both sides.  
Create an inner lining 5 mm wider than the pocket, aligning with the outer edge.  
Complete the belt cover shape.  

Use the Looping tool (shortcut I) to create panel frames for the pocket and belt cover by selecting the edges and right-clicking to hook as panels.  
Delete unused lines and points to clean up the workspace.  

Sew the pocket and belt cover to the main panel using the Free Sewing tool.  
Sew the top line of the pocket and belt cover; avoid sewing the bottom line to keep the pocket open.  
Use the Edit Pattern tool to find precise sewing start and end points.  

Separate the pocket panel from the main panel by selecting the division lines, right-clicking, and choosing Cut and Sew.  
Delete the sewing relationship between the panels to enable opening.  
Move the pocket opening section down slightly in 2D.  
Cut off about 10 mm from the opening line and delete the extra small panel.  

In 3D, the pocket design is complete and functional.  
Repeat the process symmetrically on the left side by duplicating panels and sewing.  

Add buttons and buttonholes on the big body panel, ensuring consistent positioning with the pocket cover.  
Set distances and intervals for button placement.  
Use the Button tool to add buttons and eyes, then convert buttons to eyes and copy symmetrically.  
Simulate and update the 3D model.  

Hide basic or internal lines to tidy the view.  

Add double-layer structures for parts like the cover, placket, and collar.  
Right-click parts and assign layers for symmetrical and double-layer effects.  
The internal lines are automatically sewn together.  

For fabric selection, view the shrink chart and download needed fabrics.  
Choose fabric based on desired properties.  
After changing fabric, remodel the garment to apply new physical properties.  

Adjust garment posture to a straight or A-pose before simulation.  
Simulate and adjust shrink rates gradually to avoid clipping between layers.  

Apply water-washing effects by selecting different preset types such as plain wash, speed wash, stone wash, acid wash, flushing, and smell wash.  
Each has adjustable parameters like softening, absorption, duration, intensity, and color deviation.  

Use stickers (PNG textures) for water-wash patterns and apply them to areas like elbows, pockets, and seams.  
Adjust sticker size, angle, opacity, and blending mode (e.g., mix with fabric) for realistic effects.  

Add double-needle stitching and seam lines with the Seamstress tool to simulate sewing details.  
Apply water-washing materials to edges such as collar, door frame, and pocket edges for realism.  

Save custom water-wash presets as TPT files for reuse.  
Apply pleating and edge water-washing effects to enhance realism.  

Convert buttons to metal material presets like retro copper or silver and unify their color and texture.  
Adjust button and eye positions slightly for realistic placement.  

Use the library to manage fabrics and water-wash materials efficiently.  
Open and close the library window with shortcut Y.  

Adjust the back side color of fabric separately to simulate lighter or different shades on the inside.  
Flip fabric faces on sleeves, collars, and other parts as needed to show correct fabric sides.  

Change garment posture for final display (e.g., A-pose).  
Untie buttons for open styles and adjust panel layers to prevent clipping during simulation.  

Save different versions of the project to avoid overwriting originals.  

Import additional items like pants, tops, and accessories, set their layers and shrink rates for proper fitting and simulation.  

Add background scenes from the library or download from Business City for rendering environments.  

Render the final scene using the built-in render engine.  
Adjust render size, resolution, lighting, and environment maps (HDR) for realistic lighting.  

Use skylight and environment settings to add natural lighting and shadows.  
Adjust light intensity and angle to enhance the scene.  

For advanced rendering techniques, refer to previous live classes on rendering available on Bilibili or related platforms.  

This completes the tutorial on creating a denim water-wash costume with detailed construction, fabric effects, and rendering setup.  
Thank you.

chunks.content: ## Overview of Denim Water-Wash Costume Creation in CLO This section explains the complete workflow for creating a denim water-wash costume in CLO 3D software, detailing pattern modifications, panel sewing, fabric selection, water-wash effect application, and rendering techniques. Key terms include Edit Pattern tool, sewing methods, water-wash presets, fabric shrink rates, and rendering environment settings. --- ## Initial Setup and Basic Shirt Modification This section covers importing base materials, pattern editing, and structural modification of a basic shirt into a denim jacket, focusing on panel adjustments and dimension precision. - Open CLO app and import downloaded denim water-wash materials. - Import a basic shirt file as the base garment. - Modify garment style by: - Adding a single panel at the bottom. - Widening the placket. - Dividing the upper and front body vertically. - Adding two vertical cuts on the lower half. - Designing pocket and belt cover panels. ### Pattern Adjustment Procedure - Use the Edit Pattern tool to shorten or lengthen the shirt by selecting bottom edges and moving them vertically; input specific distances (e.g., 55 mm). - Measure total bottom edge length (example: 638.2 mm) with Edit Pattern tool (shortcut Z). - Redraw the new bottom panel using the Shape tool (S) with the measured length. - Align and sew the bottom panel to front and back panels using Free Sewing or Segment Sewing. - Duplicate sewn halves symmetrically to maintain garment uniformity. - Use the Adjustment Pattern tool to position panels accurately before simulating the garment in 3D. --- ## Adding Buttons and Modifying the Placket This section explains how to add buttons/buttonholes, adjust placket width, and apply precise measurements for placement to ensure symmetry and realism. - Identify the placket's midpoint; buttons are placed 20 mm from the edge. - Use the Button tool in the 3D toolbar to add left-side buttons. - Set button distances from top and bottom edges (e.g., 20 mm from left, 27.5 mm from top). - Convert buttons to eyes and duplicate symmetrically. - Connect buttons and eyes using the Button tool to simulate button-eye locking. - To widen a narrow placket: - Merge existing division lines with Edit Pattern tool (Z). - Set new placket width to 40 mm (e.g., 20 mm + 20 mm). - Draw new vertical division lines using the Internal Multi-Line tool (G) while holding Shift. - Finalize with Cut and Sew command. --- ## Front Panel Segmentation and Pocket/Belt Cover Design This section focuses on dividing the front panel into upper/lower segments, creating pockets and belt covers, and refining panel shapes for a realistic garment structure. - Use Hook and Loop tool to cut and sew hollow lines on the front panel. - Draw horizontal inner lines with Internal Multi-Line tool for placket finishing. - Smooth division lines using Curve Edit tool by converting corners to curves or deleting excess points.

chunks.content: --- ## Front Panel Segmentation and Pocket/Belt Cover Design This section focuses on dividing the front panel into upper/lower segments, creating pockets and belt covers, and refining panel shapes for a realistic garment structure. - Use Hook and Loop tool to cut and sew hollow lines on the front panel. - Draw horizontal inner lines with Internal Multi-Line tool for placket finishing. - Smooth division lines using Curve Edit tool by converting corners to curves or deleting excess points. - Divide the lower front panel vertically with Plus Point Division tool (shortcut X): - Input specific segment lengths (e.g., 65 mm, 25 mm for lower line; 30 mm, 90 mm for upper line). - Draw pocket patterns wider than vertical dividing lines. - Use Plus Point Division tool to set pocket height (e.g., 125 mm). - Set internal line diameters to 10 mm without extension to ensure closed shapes. - Adjust pocket shape and position in 3D by enabling inner line display and using Control key to create elliptical curves, extending edges 10 mm outward. - Create belt cover similarly with diameters 30 mm and 20 mm; add 5 mm wider lining. - Use Looping tool (shortcut I) to create panel frames by hooking edges as panels. - Clean workspace by deleting unused lines and points. --- ## Sewing and Panel Separation Techniques This section provides instructions on sewing panels and creating functional openings, especially for pockets, to maintain garment realism. - Sew pocket and belt cover to main panel using Free Sewing tool: - Sew only top edges; leave bottom edges unsewn to keep pocket opening. - Use Edit Pattern tool to identify precise sewing start/end points. - Separate pocket panel by selecting division lines and using Cut and Sew. - Delete sewing relationships between pocket and main panel to allow opening. - Slightly move pocket opening down in 2D. - Trim about 10 mm from the opening line and delete small excess panels. - Duplicate and symmetrically sew panels on the opposite side. - Add buttons and buttonholes on the main body panel aligned with pocket covers, maintaining consistent intervals. - Finalize by simulating and updating the 3D garment. --- ## Double-Layer Structures and Fabric Management This section discusses creating double-layer effects on parts like covers and collars, managing fabric properties, and preparing garments for physical simulation. - Add double layers by right-clicking parts and assigning layers for symmetrical effects. - Internal lines are automatically sewn between layers. - Access shrink charts to select fabrics with desired stretch and shrink properties. - After fabric assignment, remodel the garment to apply physical fabric properties. - Set garment posture to straight or A-pose before simulation. - Gradually adjust shrink rates to prevent clipping between layers during simulation. --- ## Applying Water-Wash Effects and Texture Stickers This section covers the application of various water-wash presets, sticker textures, and material adjustments to simulate realistic denim washing effects.

Gradually adjust shrink rates to prevent clipping between layers during simulation. --- ## Applying Water-Wash Effects and Texture Stickers This section covers the application of various water-wash presets, sticker textures, and material adjustments to simulate realistic denim washing effects. - Select from water-wash presets such as plain wash, speed wash, stone wash, acid wash, flushing, and smell wash. - Adjust parameters including: - Softening - Absorption - Duration - Intensity - Color deviation - Apply PNG sticker textures to targeted areas (e.g., elbows, pockets, seams). - Customize sticker attributes: size, angle, opacity, blending mode (e.g., mix with fabric). - Add double-needle stitching and seam lines with the Seamstress tool to enhance sewing detail realism. - Apply water-wash materials to edges (collar, door frame, pocket edges). - Save custom water-wash presets as TPT files for reuse. - Add pleating and edge water-washing effects for enhanced texture realism. --- ## Button Material and Position Adjustment This section explains how to convert buttons to metal materials and refine their placement for authenticity. - Convert buttons to metal presets such as retro copper or silver. - Unify button color and texture for consistency. - Slightly adjust button and eye positions to improve realism. - Use the fabric and water-wash material library to manage resources efficiently. - Open/close library window with shortcut Y. --- ## Fabric Face Management and Final Garment Posture This section details controlling fabric side visibility and final garment posing for presentation. - Adjust fabric back side color separately to simulate lighter or different shades inside the garment. - Flip fabric faces on sleeves, collars, and other parts to display correct fabric sides. - Change garment posture to A-pose or other styles for final display. - Untie buttons and adjust panel layers to prevent clipping during simulation. - Save multiple project versions to avoid overwriting originals. --- ## Importing Additional Garments and Scene Setup This section describes adding complementary items and setting up scenes for realistic rendering. - Import items such as pants, tops, and accessories. - Assign layers and adjust shrink rates for proper fitting and simulation. - Add background scenes from built-in library or download from Business City for environment settings. - Use built-in render engine for final scene rendering. - Adjust render settings including: - Size and resolution - Lighting and shadow intensity - Environment maps (HDR) for natural lighting - Utilize skylight and environment settings to enhance lighting quality. - Adjust light intensity and angle to optimize scene realism. - For advanced rendering techniques, refer to related live classes on platforms like Bilibili. --- ## Summary This tutorial comprehensively covers denim water-wash costume creation in CLO 3D, from initial pattern modifications and sewing to fabric selection, water-wash effect application, button detailing, and final rendering setup.
